blocks.x: As a prequel to 1980’s Friday The 13th, which spawned 11 more movies, including a Nightmare On Elm Street crossover and a 2009 reboot, Peacock’s Crystal Lake isn’t aiming for originality. It features the horror franchise’s familiar ingredients, like horny and doomed camp counselors dying gruesomely in the atmospheric New Jersey woods and a stellar theme song composed by Harry Manfredini, who scored 10 of the films. What sets Crystal Lake apart, for better and worse, is that it isn’t relentless kills shoved into a digestible 95-minute runtime. The lengthy eight-episode season exists to flesh out Pamela Voorhees (Linda Cardellini, taking over the role from Betsy Palmer), who audiences barely met before she was decapitated at the end of Friday The 13th and her son took over as a masked killer. In giving her a distressing backstory that spins its wheels, Crystal Lake successfully deepens the character, but messes with the franchise’s mythology.

If the first few films were slaughterfests that hardly touched upon any larger iconoclastic themes (considering most of the victims were independent youth subverting authority and engaging in drugs and premarital sex at camp), then the show’s ethos is a try-hard “monsters aren’t born, they’re made.” Series creator Brad Caleb Kane reframes Friday The 13th‘s lore with a more modern-day horror mindset of grief as the true monster. (A line from the show, “trauma actually makes him stronger,” refers to Jason, but it applies to his mom as well). The franchise alters the lore and timeline, changing the year of Jason Voorhees’ (Chucky‘s Callum Vinson) accidental drowning from 1957 to 1971. Before he “dies,” the show offers a glimpse at Pamela and Jason’s sweet, candid relationship. Witnessing a still-alive, cute-as-a-button Jason is a huge change in itself, helping Crystal Lake humanize the antagonists and establish its purpose as a Voorhees family origin story.

Crystal Lake naturally raises the question: Is this necessary? Are Pamela and Jason better off as bitter and isolated villains, wielding whatever weapon they find to hurt anyone who crosses their paths? The show doesn’t paint them just as vengeance-fueled serial killers; it demands empathy for them by depicting how Pamela fought against dark, corrupt institutional forces before moving to Crystal Lake for a fresh start. But even in this New Jersey town, they’re outcasts. A disfigured Jason gets bullied, while Pam’s only mission is to protect her son. She’s shattered when, while working at the camp as a chef, she witnesses her kid sink to the bottom of the lake. Nine months later, her sorrow gradually morphs into homicidal rage when the camp reopens against her wishes. No one listens to her pleas that Jason might still be out there because his body was never found.

Kane pushes a plethora of ideas in Crystal Lake that don’t always seamlessly blend. The show wants to understand Pamela’s grief and how it reshaped her identity, touching on how she lives in an era of women’s rights movements and the rise of the hippie culture—Camp Crystal Lake’s attendees in 1972 include the most broadly written, weed-consuming nonconformists. In Jason’s absence, Pamela doesn’t immediately open up to her peers like Rita (Joy Suprano) or Sheriff Levon Brooks (William Catlett), who harbors a crush on her. Instead, she latches onto a lonely young girl/Jason’s only friend, Grace (Gwendolyn Sundstrom), hoping to fill a void in both their lives. The writers commendably mine Pamela’s pathologically obsessive nature through this surprising arc, although, again, they play with Friday The 13th‘s lore too much, including its opening scene with frisky camp counselors Barry (Phoenix Parvenik) and Claudette (Danielle Kotch).

Crystal Lake sometimes acts as a promising small-town psychological thriller, expanding on how familiar faces like a younger Crazy Ralph (Nick Cordileone) and police officer Dorf (Cameron Scoggins) deal with dead bodies popping up all over. It’s only when Pam’s past properly catches up to her that the series gets unwieldy and loses momentum, drawing from other horror favorites like Frankenstein. But Crystal Lake is still immensely watchable because it’s anchored by an exceptional—and exceptionally gonzo—lead performance. In a sharp turn from her Emmy–winning deadpan work in DTF St. Louis earlier this year, Cardellini loudly and proudly unleashes Pamela’s paranoia and pain in her facial expressions and bodily movements, making Pam’s descent into madness inevitable and palpable without getting campy. The show’s other indisputable MVP is the makeup and prosthetics department; their technical prowess makes Crystal Lake an utterly gnarly slasher.

Admittedly, most of the films are about Pam’s son, who has a convoluted journey going from a killing machine to a supernatural entity. Crystal Lake nods to that evolution by the end, but for the most part, it’s rooted in Pamela’s bizarre yet grounded tale. None of it is exactly inventive, but Crystal Lake‘s jump scares and character study make for a gory ride.
Crystal Lake premieres October 15 on Peacock.
Saloni Gajjar is The A.V. Club‘s TV critic.
